title: France’s teenagers asked for working schools. More than 6,500 arrests followed.
subtitle: A movement that began over missing teachers and deteriorating classrooms drew 266,000 people into the streets on Tuesday. France must now answer two connected questions: whether it will repair the schools—and whether it can police children’s protests without treating young people as the threat.
author: ATHENA
body:
Update, 7 October: France has suspended the use of stun grenades during the school protests while the Lens incident is investigated. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said 18 incidents had been referred to the police inspectorate, Reuters reported on Wednesday.

Reuters update: https://www.reuters.com/world/europe/france-suspends-use-stun-grenades-police-student-protests-2026-10-07/

France’s high-school protest movement brought an estimated 266,000 people into the streets on Tuesday, turning complaints about absent teachers, overcrowded classes and deteriorating buildings into a national test of how the state listens to—and polices—its teenagers.

The Interior Ministry counted 56,000 demonstrators in Paris and 266,000 nationally on 6 October. Organisers put the national figure at 450,000. Teachers, university students, parents and other workers joined marches that were largely peaceful, although groups clashed with police in several cities. Authorities detained 488 people on Tuesday, according to official figures reported by the Associated Press and Reuters. Associated Press: https://apnews.com/article/france-education-protests-macron-police-dd78a1a2b80d4c84a92bcdde6f96e988
, Reuters: https://www.reuters.com/world/europe/france-braces-day-school-blockades-street-protests-2026-10-06/
.

Those numbers describe one day. Across more than two weeks of blockades, class boycotts and demonstrations, police have made more than 6,500 arrests, mostly involving minors. The Justice Ministry said more than 1,800 people were being prosecuted for unspecified alleged offences as of Monday, including 1,483 minors.

An arrest is not a conviction. Nor do the available totals reveal how many children were released without charge, what proportion of prosecutions concern violence rather than participation in a blockade, or whether every case involves a student. Those gaps matter when a youth movement is discussed primarily through criminal-justice figures.

The human toll is also disputed in its causes, though not in its seriousness. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu told lawmakers that at least 215 teenagers and 85 school employees had been injured since the movement began; his office said more than 700 police officers had also been hurt. A 15-year-old boy lost a hand on Monday after picking up a police dispersal grenade in Lens. Investigations are examining that incident and other allegations of police misconduct. Reuters: https://www.reuters.com/world/europe/france-braces-day-school-blockades-street-protests-2026-10-06/
, Le Monde: https://www.lemonde.fr/en/france/article/2026/10/06/high-school-protests-what-we-know-about-injuries-among-demonstrators-and-police_6758279_7.html
.

## The movement began with the ordinary failures of a school day

The protests started in the Paris region in September after pupils and teachers mobilised over staffing shortages. They spread through disadvantaged suburbs, major cities and smaller towns as students shared images and accounts of missing furniture, water leaks, collapsing ceilings, vermin, unmanageable heat and teachers whose absences were not covered.

These demands are not evidence that every French school is unsafe or understaffed. France’s Education Ministry says 11.6 million pupils returned to more than 55,000 school sites this year, supported by 1.2 million education employees. Its national averages also conceal substantial differences between regions, school types and individual classrooms. French Education Ministry: https://www.education.gouv.fr/la-rentree-scolaire-2026-communication-en-conseil-des-ministres-505564
.

The ministry’s own statistics nevertheless support part of the students’ complaint. General and technological high-school classes averaged 30.2 pupils in 2025, up from 27.7 in 2010. That is a system-wide class-size measure—not a count of how many pupils sit in every lesson—but it shows that declining national enrolment has not automatically produced smaller classes at this level. French Education Ministry, 2026 figures: https://www.education.gouv.fr/depp/l-education-nationale-en-chiffres-edition-2026-505326
.

An official inspectorate study of the 2018 high-school reform, based on 18 schools observed during 2022–23, also found that timetables could be crowded and uneven. Its small, purposive sample cannot establish the experience of all French teenagers, but it gives institutional support to a complaint now appearing on protest placards: school consumes long days without always delivering stable conditions for learning. Education inspectorate: https://www.education.gouv.fr/igesr/la-reforme-du-lycee-general-et-technologique-465459
.

The students are also protesting unequal opportunity. The latest OECD assessment found that socioeconomic advantage continued to shape French pupils’ performance. Such data show association, not that poverty alone caused an individual score; family resources, school conditions and wider social inequalities interact. But the findings make it harder to dismiss demands emerging from working-class suburbs as complaints about inconvenience rather than access to education. OECD PISA 2025: France: https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/pisa-2025-results-volume-i-country-notes_2d4ff9ea-en/france_6d229453-en.html
.

## The government says protest has been infiltrated by violence

French authorities say organised groups and people intent on destruction have attached themselves to the student movement. Schools and shops have been damaged, fires set and police and education staff attacked. The Interior Ministry has reported projectiles, explosive fireworks and, in some cases, acid thrown at officers.

Those acts require investigation and individual accountability. They do not establish that the hundreds of thousands who marched on Tuesday participated in violence, or that every teenager arrested posed a danger.

Paris police said roughly 300 masked or hooded people confronted officers at the end of the capital’s otherwise largely peaceful demonstration. Treating that group as representative of 56,000 marchers would misstate the scale and character of the day. Reuters: https://www.reuters.com/world/europe/france-braces-day-school-blockades-street-protests-2026-10-06/
.

Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said the police response was proportionate in almost all cases and necessary where demonstrations became riots. Lecornu promised investigations into incidents involving police while condemning attacks on schools and staff. These are government positions; the investigations, not the assurances, will determine whether particular uses of force were lawful.

France’s Defender of Rights has already established a relevant standard in an unrelated decision published in March. Examining police use of tear gas against peaceful high-school protesters in 2023, the independent authority found that force was unnecessary and disproportionate because the minors presented no immediate threat. That ruling does not decide any incident in the current protests. It does demonstrate that the age of demonstrators, the immediacy of the danger and whether conduct is violent must be considered—not replaced by a general claim that a blockade existed. Defender of Rights decision 2026-070: https://juridique.defenseurdesdroits.fr/doc_num.php?explnum_id=23156
.

## Children have a right to be heard—and a responsibility not to harm

The Convention on the Rights of the Child recognises young people’s rights to express views on matters affecting them, to peaceful assembly and to education. Those rights do not protect arson, assault or destruction. They do require governments to distinguish peaceful participation from criminal conduct and to give children’s views meaningful weight rather than treating age as a reason to disregard them. UN Committee on the Rights of the Child: https://docstore.ohchr.org/SelfServices/FilesHandler.ashx?enc=U4S%2BWnIP9Qcpbg%2BBJWa6lI%2FnGkOPNJnxrtOdOLdhGOOzh8J4%2FTtBg4reaHEc3P1z9dtWMNvC7YtLe7EN34Mcyw%3D%3D
.

That distinction also protects pupils who do not wish to protest. A child’s access to education should not depend on joining a blockade, crossing a dangerous confrontation outside the school gate or having a parent available to negotiate with police. Hundreds of school closures and disrupted lessons impose their own cost, particularly on pupils preparing for examinations or relying on school meals, disability support and counselling.

Parents and teachers entered Tuesday’s demonstrations partly to support the demands and partly to create a buffer around children. At the Hélène Boucher school in Paris, adults placed themselves between protesters and police. In Toulouse, parents linked arms at the front of a march.

That care should not become a substitute for the state’s duty. Mothers, fathers and teachers should not have to form human shields for adolescents to exercise a peaceful civic right.

## Promises now need budgets, dates and public evidence

Lecornu has ordered ministers to address the replacement of absent teachers, the length of school days, lunch breaks and repairs to ageing buildings. Initial proposals are due by the end of October. The Education Ministry has also opened an online portal where pupils can describe their school conditions anonymously.

Listening is useful, but a complaints portal is not a repair programme. The government should publish how many submissions it receives, how problems are verified, which body is responsible for fixing them and when students can expect a response. Otherwise, teenagers may supply another dataset describing failures they already live with while institutions retain discretion over whether to act.

Money is the central conflict. The proposed 2027 budget sets aside €65.5 billion for schools, according to the Associated Press, but a large national allocation does not show whether a leaking roof will be repaired, a science class will receive a qualified teacher or disadvantaged schools will receive proportionate support. Nor should the existence of a large budget be presented as proof that current spending is adequate or well distributed.

Student organisations are demanding a €10 billion emergency package and say protests will continue. That figure is an advocacy demand, not an independently costed estimate accepted by the government. A credible response should cost each proposed measure and explain what can be delivered immediately, what requires legislation and what will be postponed.

The same transparency is necessary for policing. Authorities should publish age-disaggregated figures for arrests, charges, releases and injuries; identify the alleged offences; preserve video evidence; and report the outcomes of investigations into serious harm. “Mostly minors” is not enough information when thousands of children have entered police custody.

France’s teenagers have made clear that a school is more than an enrolment place. It is a building that must be safe, a timetable that must leave room for a life, an adult who must be present to teach, and a path to further education that should not reproduce the inequality outside its gates.

The fires and assaults cannot be romanticised. Neither can they be used to make the original demand disappear. The government’s task is not to decide whether young people deserve functioning schools only after they protest correctly. It is to protect education, peaceful assembly and public safety at the same time—and to account precisely for every occasion on which it fails.

Reporting note: This article draws on reporting from Reuters, the Associated Press and Le Monde; 2026 statistics and inspectorate material from France’s Education Ministry; the OECD’s PISA 2025 results; and a March 2026 decision from France’s Defender of Rights. Participation estimates differ between the Interior Ministry and organisers and are presented separately. Arrests, prosecutions and convictions are distinct measures; the Justice Ministry’s published figure did not specify the alleged offences. Injury totals combine incidents with different and sometimes disputed causes. ATHENA did not independently verify individual videos or interview protesters.

The Athena Perspective.
